content: The longer treatment regimens (18–20 months) remained an option for patients who were not eligible for shorter regimens. Modifications to these treatment protocols prompted the World Health Organization (WHO) to evaluate new evidence, leading to updated recommendations that balanced the effectiveness and potential harms of new or modified regimens. Efforts to reduce the duration of treatment for multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (MDR/RR-TB) have driven initiatives to treat patients with shorter regimens under both programmatic and trial conditions. When carefully selected patients with MDR/RR-TB, who had no prior exposure to second-line drugs or additional resistance to these drugs, were treated with these shorter regimens, relapse-free cure rates of approximately 80% or higher were achieved, even under programmatic conditions. In 2016, based on observational data from standardized shorter regimens in African and Asian countries, WHO recommended a standardized 9–12-month shorter MDR-TB regimen for eligible patients. In 2018, following the results of the STREAM Stage 1 trial, WHO revised its recommendations for shorter MDR-TB regimens, including replacing the injectable agent kanamycin (or capreomycin) with amikacin. Evidence of permanent toxic effects from injectable agents has driven the development of shorter, injectable-sparing regimens. South Africa’s Department of Health shared observational data with WHO on a 9-month all-oral bedaquiline-containing regimen, which WHO reviewed and recommended in 2019. This regimen included bedaquiline (used for 6 months) combined with levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, ethionamide, ethambutol, high-dose isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and clofazimine for 4 months (extendable to 6 months if the patient remained sputum smear-positive at 4 months), followed by 5 months of levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, clofazimine, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. The urgent need for more effective treatment regimens for patients with extensive drug resistance, including fluoroquinolone resistance, has led to studies testing novel regimens with newer and repurposed drugs. One of the first studies, the Nix-TB study by the TB Alliance, was a Phase 3, open-label observational cohort study conducted in South Africa between 2014 and 2019. It evaluated the safety, efficacy, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of a 6-month bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL) regimen, extendable to 9 months for patients who missed doses or reverted to culture-positive status. The study provided evidence reviewed by WHO in 2019, leading to recommendations for the BPaL regimen in pre-XDR-TB patients under operational research conditions. Two randomized controlled trials (RCTs), TB-PRACTECAL and ZeNix, concluded in 2021 and provided new evidence prompting WHO to update its MDR/RR-TB treatment guidelines. The 2022 WHO guidelines included recommendations for 6-month regimens, linezolid dosing, and modified 9-month regimens. Evidence for these updates came from close collaboration with national TB programs, researchers, and the TB Alliance. Data from the TB-PRACTECAL trial supported the use of BPaLM (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and moxifloxacin) and BPaL regimens, while the ZeNix trial provided insights into linezolid dosing. Programmatic data from South Africa supported the use of a new 9-month shorter regimen. The NExT trial, a Phase 2–3 open-label RCT in South Africa, evaluated a 6–9-month all-oral regimen compared to the local standard of care. However, due to early trial termination and variability in intervention components, its data could not be fully integrated into WHO’s guideline discussions. Despite this, the trial highlighted the inferiority and worse safety profile of injectable-based regimens compared to all-oral regimens. Importantly, it demonstrated that better outcomes could be achieved with a 6-month all-oral regimen than with traditional 9-month or longer injectable-based regimens. WHO’s consolidated guidelines on drug-resistant TB treatment, updated in 2022, recommend a 6-month BPaLM regimen over longer regimens for MDR/RR-TB patients. This recommendation is based on evidence showing improved treatment success rates (89% with BPaLM compared to 52% with standard regimens), fewer adverse events with lower linezolid doses, and feasibility and cost-effectiveness of implementation. The 6-month BPaLM regimen is now considered the preferred option for eligible patient groups.
